newsitem.title: USA: January retail sales up after lackluster December.
newsitem.headline: January retail sales up after lackluster December.

text.p: Sales at retail stores rebounded moderately in January from a December holiday sales season that was much weaker than previously thought, the Commerce Department said on Thursday.

Total retail sales grew by 0.6 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted $209.1 billion after a steeply revised 0.3 percent gain in December. The government previously said sales in December had risen much more strongly by 0.6 percent.
Economists said the weak report would give the Federal Reserve no incentive to raise interest rates.

"You still have some decent consumer spending growth going into the first quarter, but it was not quite what was expected. People were expecting fairly stronger growth," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.

"I believe that this sort of puts yet another nail in the coffin" of expectations for the Federal Reserve tightening interest rates any time sonn, Allan Leslie, an independent economist in New York, said.
January sales excluding automobiles, which alone account for about one-quarter of all retail business, were up only 0.4 percent.
The January figures were below Wall Street economists' forecasts for an overall 0.7 percent increase and for a 0.6 percent rise excluding automobile sales.

The downward revision in December sales suggests the economy may have entered 1997 with somewhat less momentum than previously thought. Consumer purchases of goods and services account for about two-thirds of national economic activity. "It's a lot stronger than what we have been seeing ...," Michael Niemira, an economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, said.

"When you step back, it says the consumer is alive and well and continues to spend. The near-term dynamic is still favourable, but what happens toward the end of the year is a different story. The second half is when we may see a slowdown in consumption."
While January sales clearly showed a pickup in retail business, it was from a lower level in December than previously thought.
Sales of all types of long-lasting durable goods, from cars to refrigerators, were up 0.7 percent last month to $85.4 billion following a 0.2 percent gain in December.
Sales of more quickly used nondurables, like food and gasoline, increased 0.5 percent to $123.6 billion after a 0.3 percent December gain.

Sales by general merchandise stores increased during January by 1.3 percent to $26.4 billion after a 0.8 percent gain in December. But at apparel stores, sales of clothing dropped by 0.9 percent to $9.2 billion following a 0.4 percent rise in December.
Sales of building materials grew by 1.2 percent to $11.2 billion in January following a 0.8 percent decline in December.
Furniture sales were up by 0.6 percent to $11.4 billion after a 0.8 percent drop in December.

Sales by food stores were flat in January at $35.8 billion after a small 0.2 percent December increase while gasoline sales posted a strong 0.9 percent gain to $13.5 billion following a 0.4 percent December increase.
